t: Minimum Operations to Exceed Threshold Value I
o: Each operation removes one occurrence of the current smallest element; we need every remaining element to be ≥ k. Clearly we should only ever remove elements smaller than k — removing anything ≥ k is wasted work. In Example 1 with k = 10, the elements 1, 2, 3 are below 10 and must each be removed (three operations), while 11 and 10 stay. In Example 2 nothing is below k = 1, so zero operations suffice. In Example 3, four of five elements are below 9. Hence the answer is simply the count of elements strictly less than k.
k: Only elements < k ever need removal, and each requires exactly one operation.
The guaranteed existence of an element ≥ k ensures the process terminates successfully.

a.i: Every element below k must eventually be deleted, and deleting it takes exactly one operation; elements ≥ k never need to be touched. So the minimum number of operations equals the number of elements strictly less than k.
s: Count elements x with x < k.
a.t: O(n) — a single scan of the array.

a.i: Equivalently, sort the array and locate the first index whose value is ≥ k (via binary search); everything before that index must be removed. This framing generalizes naturally to variants where removals have costs or thresholds change between queries.
s: Binary search for the leftmost position with value ≥ k (bisect_left / lower_bound).
Return that position — the number of elements below k.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting; the binary search is O(log n).
a.sp: O(1) or O(sort) auxiliary space depending on the sort implementation.

w: Use the O(n) counting approach — it is optimal and trivially correct. The sorted/binary-search version is worth mentioning as the pattern to reach for in harder variants (e.g. per-query thresholds or weighted removals). Pitfalls: use strict comparison x < k (elements equal to k are fine to keep), and note the problem guarantees at least one element ≥ k so the answer never equals n. A likely follow-up is the 'II' version where each operation merges the two smallest elements, requiring a min-heap.
